Two questions today: what is the unit of text? . what numbers should a token become?
what is the unit of text?
1. From Text to Tokens | Models Don't Read
• What a computer actually sees: bytes - "ChatGPT는 똑똑해" = EC 9E 90 EC 97 B0 … (UTF-8)
• What a neural network actually eats: integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary - [8203, 318, 15339, …]
• The bridge between them is the tokenizer: text → token sequence → ID sequence
• The design question: what goes into the vocabulary? Words? Characters? Something in between?
• This one choice shapes model quality, cost, and multilingual ability
Tokenization is the first decision every NLP system makes - and it is surprisingly hard
1. From Text to Tokens | Option 1 - Words
• The natural first answer: split on spaces - "I love NLP" → [I, love, NLP]
• Problem 1 - OOV (out-of-vocabulary): anything not in the vocab becomes [UNK] - new words, typos, names all die
- "갓생", "억텐", “야르”, "ChatGPT" - none of these existed in a 2012 vocabulary
• Problem 2 - vocabulary explosion: "run"/"runs"/"running"/"ran" are all separate words - a disaster for morphology-
• Problem 3 - lost structure: "unbelievable" and "believe" end up as totally unrelated IDs
Word-level looks natural - and breaks immediately in the real world
1. From Text to Tokens | The Long Tail - Zipf's Law
• Zipf's law: frequency � 1/rank - a handful of words dominate the corpus, and most words barely appear
• However big you make the vocabulary, the tail gets cut - and the cut tail all becomes [UNK]
You cannot enumerate a language - the vocabulary must be built, not listed
1. From Text to Tokens | Option 2 - Characters
• The opposite extreme: characters - "love" → [l, o, v, e]
• Pros: tiny vocabulary (a few hundred), and OOV is impossible by construction
• Con 1: sequences get long - 5× longer text means 5²× = 25× more attention compute later
• Con 2: the unit is meaningless - 'l' and 'o' stand for nothing
- the model must first re-learn how to assemble meaning out of letters
Characters solve OOV but pay for it in sequence length and meaningless units
1. From Text to Tokens | Option 3 - Subwords
• The modern answer: frequent chunks stay whole, rare words break into pieces
• unbelievable → un + believ + able 자연어처리는 → 자연어 + 처리 + 는
• Frequent "the" or "안녕하세요" = one token - unseen "Kyzylorda" still spellable from pieces
• No OOV + reasonable sequence length + meaningful units - all three at once
• The remaining question: who decides which pieces enter the vocabulary? Let the data decide!
Every modern LLM - GPT, Claude, Llama, EXAONE - tokenizes with subwords
1. From Text to Tokens | BPE - The Algorithm
• Byte-Pair Encoding (Sennrich et al. 2016 - originally a 1994 compression algorithm)
1. Initialize the vocabulary with characters (or bytes)
2. Find the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus
3. Merge that pair into a new token; record the merge rule
4. Repeat 2-3 until the vocabulary reaches the target size
• What gets learned is an ordered list of merge rules - that list IS the tokenizer
No linguistics, no hand-written rules - just “count and merge”, repeated
1. From Text to Tokens | BPE - Worked Example
• Toy corpus: low ×5 . lower ×2 . newest ×6 . widest ×3 (</w> marks end-of-word)
In today's lab you implement exactly this algorithm in ~20 lines of Python
1. From Text to Tokens | Applying BPE . Byte-Level BPE
• At inference: split new text into characters, then replay the learned merges in the same order
- lowest → l.o.w.e.s.t → (es) → (est) → (lo) → low + est - unseen words still work
• Byte-level BPE (standard since GPT-2): start from the 256 bytes instead of characters
• Emoji, hanja, Arabic, typos - any input is bytes, so UNK simply cannot exist
• GPT-4o, Llama, and Claude all use byte-level BPE-family tokenizers
Train once on data - then every future string, in every language, is tokenizable
1. From Text to Tokens | WordPiece & Unigram
• WordPiece (BERT): merge the pair that most increases corpus likelihood, not raw frequency - continuation pieces get ##
• Unigram LM : the reverse - start big, prune the least useful pieces
- each sentence is tokenized as its highest-probability segmentation - a probabilistic view
• SentencePiece: treats whitespace as just another symbol (�) - great for languages with unreliable spacing (Korean,
• Practical intuition: all three share one philosophy - “frequent chunks become tokens”
Start with small units →repeatedly merge frequent pairs
Start with small units →merge based on a score that best explains the corpus
Start with a large candidate vocabulary →repeatedly remove less useful pieces
BPE . WordPiece . Unigram - three recipes, one philosophy
1. From Text to Tokens | Tokenizers in the Wild
• Real vocabulary sizes: GPT-2 50k → Llama 3 128k → GPT-4o ~200k - growing to embrace more languages
• Special tokens: <|endoftext|>, [CLS], [SEP], chat-template tokens - switches that steer model behavior
• Tokens = money: API pricing and context limits are all counted in tokens - tokenizer efficiency is cost
• Tokens = blind spots: why LLMs miscount the r's in "strawberry" - the model sees str + awberry, never letters
- numbers split oddly too (12345 → 123 + 45) - one reason LLM arithmetic gets weird
Half of the “weird LLM failures” you meet online are tokenizer artifacts
cutting an agglutinative language into subwords
• Korean is agglutinative - grammatical morphemes stack onto a stem to form one word (어절)
• Splitting on spaces is the worst case: 먹었겠더라 / 먹었더라 / 먹겠더라 … all become different "words"
Last week's preview becomes today's main act - the unit problem is far worse in Korean
• Morphological analyzers (형태소 분석기): use linguistic knowledge to split words into morphemes + POS tags
- 자연어처리는 재미있다 → 자연어/NNG + 처리/NNG + 는/JX + 재미있/VA + 다/EF
• Tools: MeCab-ko, Kiwi, Okt, Komoran - the classic workhorses of Korean NLP
• Pros: linguistically clean units . particles/endings split precisely . strong for search & classification
• Cons: analyzer mistakes propagate into every later stage . weak on slang & new words . dictionaries need maintenance
Linguistically beautiful - but a rule-based system with rule-based weaknesses
2. Korean Tokenization | Route 2 - Subwords on Korean
• What if we just run BPE on a Korean corpus? It works - surprisingly well
• Frequent words (안녕하세요) stay whole; inflections split near stem/ending boundaries on their own
• Choice of starting unit: syllables (가.각.간…) . jamo (ㄱ.ㅏ…) . bytes
- syllable-start is the practical standard - jamo/bytes can shatter one character into 2-3 tokens
• Caveat: a tokenizer trained on English-heavy data shreds Korean into byte crumbs →(see the next slide)
BPE knows no linguistics - but if the data is Korean, it learns Korean . only if the data is Korean
• Fertility = average tokens per word - how "expensively" a tokenizer treats a language
• Same meaning, same sentence - Korean pays 2-3× more tokens:
Same API, same context window - Korean users pay double . this is why Korean tokenizers exist
2. Korean Tokenization | What Korean Models Actually Do
• Recipe 1 - train your own BPE/Unigram on a Korean-heavy corpus (the most common answer)
• Recipe 2 - morpheme-aware subwords: pre-split with an analyzer, then run BPE - a hybrid of both routes
- cutting particle/ending boundaries first helps BPE learn cleaner pieces
• Recipe 3 - multilingual models grow the vocab (128k-256k) so each language gets its share
• Today's lab: train a Korean BPE tokenizer yourself with HF tokenizers, and measure its fertility
Korean tokenization is not a solved problem - it is an engineering choice you will make
meaning as a vector, learned from raw text
3. word2vec | How Do We Represent Meaning?
• What is "meaning"? The dictionary says: the idea a word represents - useless to a computer
• What we actually want: a computable object that carries meaning - comparable, composable, learnable
• Three historical attempts: a thesaurus (WordNet) → discrete symbols (one-hot) → distributional vectors
The question sounds philosophical - the answer will be a vector
• WordNet: a hand-built thesaurus of synonym sets and is-a hierarchies - classic NLP's favorite resource
- synonyms of "good", panda � bear � mammal � … hierarchies
• Problem 1: nuance is lost - is "proficient" a synonym of "good"? only in some contexts
• Problem 2: cannot keep up with new words - the fate of every human-curated resource
• Problem 3: similarity is not computable - no number for HOW similar good and marvelous are
A dictionary is a list of facts - not a computable notion of meaning
• Traditional NLP: words as discrete symbols - as vectors, that means one-hot: a single 1, everything else 0
• The fatal flaw: every pair of words is orthogonal - searching "Seattle motel" can never match "Seattle hotel"
Similarity must live inside the representation - not bolted on afterwards
• “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” - J. R. Firth, 1957
• A word's meaning = the set of contexts it appears in
• Want to know what “banking” means? Look at thousands of its contexts:
…government debt problems turning into banking crises as happened in 2009…
…saying that Europe needs unified banking regulation to replace the hodgepodge…
• The most successful idea of modern statistical NLP - word2vec, BERT, and GPT all stand on it
Meaning from context - no dictionary, no labels, just raw text
• Give every word a dense real-valued vector - typically 50-1024 dims (vs |V| dims for one-hot!)
• Design principle: similar contexts → similar vectors, similarity measured by the dot product
• Names you'll hear: word vectors = (word) embeddings = (neural) word representations - same thing
• The remaining problem: how do we LEARN these numbers? → word2vec
A word is a point in space - and geometry becomes meaning
• word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013): a framework for learning word vectors
• Ingredients: one large corpus - that's all (no labels!)
• Idea: slide a window over the text and make the center word predict its neighbors
• To predict well, the vectors are forced to absorb context - prediction is the means, vectors are the goal
• This is the prototype of self-supervised learning - the data supplies its own answers
- GPT's "predict the next token" is exactly the same philosophy
Predict the neighbors - and meaning falls out as a by-product
• Center word c at position t, context words o within window size m - slide one step and repeat
• At every position t, for every context word: adjust vectors to make P(o|c) large
One corpus → millions of tiny prediction problems, for free
• For every position t = 1 … T, multiply the probabilities of all context words in the window:
• θ = every adjustable parameter = all the word vectors
• Better vectors make the real corpus look more "plausible" - find θ that maximizes L(θ)
• A product of millions of probabilities is numerically awful → take logs and flip the sign (next slide)
The whole corpus becomes one number to maximize
• Take the log (product → sum), flip the sign (max → min), divide by T (average):
• J(θ) = average negative log-likelihood - our loss function
• Minimizing J = maximizing prediction accuracy = good word vectors
• One puzzle piece left: how do we compute P(o|c; θ) from vectors?
Minimize J - every deep learning story starts exactly like this
• word2vec's trick: give every word TWO vectors
• vw - used when w is the center word
• uw - used when w is a context word
• The "similarity" score is the dot product: uo . vc - large → o is likely near c
• Why two? It makes optimization cleaner. After training, average them or just keep v
Similarity = dot product - the single most reused idea in this course
3. word2vec | Softmax - From Scores to Probabilities
• A dot product can be any real number → we need probabilities → softmax
(1) Dot product compares similarity of o between c
• Numerator: exponentiate the score of the true context word o
• Denominator: normalize by the scores of EVERY word in the vocabulary → a proper distribution
• A "soft" "max": big scores stand out (max), small scores never hit zero (soft)
• Remember that Σ over |V| in the denominator - it will cause trouble soon
Scores in, probabilities out - softmax appears in every neural NLP model you will ever meet
• θ = all u's and v's stacked into one long vector - 2 × d × V real numbers (d=300, V=100k → 60 million)
“Training a model” = nudging these numbers until J goes down
• We want J(θ) to go down → step in the direction opposite the gradient, a little at a time
• α = learning rate - the step size. Too big: diverge. Too small: forever
•��J = the vector of partial derivatives - "which way is uphill"
• This is THE one principle behind all neural network training - GPT trains on exactly this line
• Full derivation: next week (neural foundations) + you do it by hand in A2
Walk downhill in 60-million-dimensional space - that is all “learning” is
• Problem: J sums over the entire corpus - one exact gradient means visiting billions of windows
• Fix - SGD: estimate the gradient from a few windows (a mini-batch), and step often
Noisy but fast beats exact but slow - the default of all deep learning
3. word2vec | The Gradient - One Beautiful Line
• Differentiate log P(o|c) with respect to the center vector vc (a few lines of chain rule):
• observed - the vector of the context word we actually saw, uo
• expected - the model's average context vector, Σ P(w|c) uw
• Adjust by the gap between what you saw and what you expected - learning = reducing surprise
• You derive the full thing in A2
observed - expected: this pattern returns in every classifier you will ever train
3. word2vec | Negative Sampling - The Fix for Softmax
• That Σ over |V| in the softmax - a dot product with the whole vocabulary for every single window
• Idea: stop comparing against everyone - turn it into binary classification: 1 real context word vs k random fakes
• Push σ(u.v) up for real pairs, push σ(-u.v) up for fakes - fakes sampled from freq^(3/4)
Skip-gram + negative sampling = the word2vec everyone actually runs
• Pull the real neighbor "crises" toward "banking"; push the random words away:
Pull the real neighbors closer, push random words away - repeat a billion times
• The word2vec family has two variants:
Skip-gram: better for rare words & small data - the default in papers and in this course CBOW: faster, better for frequent words

king - man + woman ≈ queen - arithmetic on meaning, learned from raw text

4. GloVe & Evaluation | Why Not Just Count?
• Isn't looping over the corpus dozens of times weird? Why not just count co-occurrences once?
The count matrix contains the same information - in a very inconvenient shape
4. GloVe & Evaluation | From Counts to Vectors - SVD & Hacks
• The classic route (LSA family): run SVD on the co-occurrence matrix X, keep the top k dims → dense low-dim vectors
• But raw counts work badly - function words (the, of) dominate everything
• The fixes: log the counts . clip with min(X, 100) . ignore function words . weight nearby words more
• Done well, this yields decent vectors (COALS etc.) - linear semantic patterns appear too
• The state of play: counting vs prediction - two camps running in parallel until 2014
Counting works too - once you beat the counts into shape
4. GloVe & Evaluation | GloVe - Best of Both Worlds
• Insight: meaning components live in ratios of co-occurrence probabilities - what separates ice/steam is their ratio with solid,
• Design: make the dot product predict the log count (weighted by f for frequent pairs):
How much do we trust it?
• Global statistics (counting) + trained optimization (prediction) - fast, and scales to huge corpora
word2vec and GloVe - the standard ingredients of NLP 2013-2018, practically tied in quality
4. GloVe & Evaluation | GloVe - What the Space Looks Like
• In the learned space, one semantic relation = one consistent vector difference:
Semantic and syntactic regularities - captured as pure geometry
• The great dichotomy of NLP evaluation - a frame we reuse all semester:
• Intrinsic: evaluate the intermediate artifact itself - analogies, similarity
- fast and diagnostic - but its link to real performance must be proven separately
• Extrinsic: plug the vectors into a real task (NER . classification . search) and measure end performance
- what actually matters - but slow, and it can't tell you WHERE the problem is
• Evidence of good vectors = plausible intrinsics + real extrinsic gains
Fast-but-indirect vs slow-but-real - you always need both
4. GloVe & Evaluation | Intrinsic Evaluation - Analogies & Similarity
• Word analogy: a : b :: c : ? - man : woman :: king : ? → argmax cos(x, b - a + c)
- Google analogy dataset: semantic (capital-country …) + syntactic (comparatives …), 19,544 questions
• Word similarity: correlation between human similarity ratings and vector cosine
• Korean counterparts exist too (WordSim-353-ko, Korean analogies) - we run in the lab
Assignment 1: you will run exactly these evaluations on your own vectors
